nodes.label: Rotational Motion
nodes.note: Rigid body dynamics: inertia, torque, angular momentum, and rolling. Translate every idea from linear mechanics by mapping m to I, F to tau, and v to omega.

nodes.label: Rigid Body Kinematics
nodes.note: Definition of a rigid body, invariance of angular velocity, and the rotational kinematic equations. Geometry of a rotating body, before any force discussion.

nodes.label: Rigid Body Definition
nodes.note: A rigid body keeps fixed inter-particle distances, so its motion is fully described by the translation of one point plus rotation about it. Every point shares the same angular velocity.

nodes.label: Invariance of Angular Velocity
nodes.note: At any instant every particle has the same $\omega$ about any fixed axis: $$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$$. Thus $\omega$ is a property of the body, not of the chosen point.

nodes.label: Rotational Kinematic Equations
nodes.note: Under constant angular acceleration the rotational analogues of the translational laws hold: $$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t,\quad \theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2,\quad \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$$. Use them exactly like the linear equations.

nodes.label: Angular Displacement
nodes.note: Angle in radians ties arc length to radius: $$\theta = \frac{s}{r},\quad v = r\omega,\quad a_t = r\alpha$$. Every circular quantity is just the linear one divided by r.

nodes.label: Centripetal Acceleration
nodes.note: Even steady rotation needs inward acceleration: $$a_c = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}$$. Total acceleration combines it with the tangential part: $$a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$.

nodes.label: Linear-Rotational Analogy
nodes.note: Every translational law has a rotational twin: $$s \leftrightarrow \theta,\ v \leftrightarrow \omega,\ m \leftrightarrow I,\ F \leftrightarrow \tau,\ p \leftrightarrow L$$. Translate a familiar result rather than memorising a new one.

nodes.label: Moment of Inertia
nodes.note: Rotational inertia about axes, radius of gyration, axis-shift theorems, and the standard values. The quantity that plays the role of mass in rotation.

nodes.label: Definition and Radius of Gyration
nodes.note: Rotational inertia is $$I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2 = \int r^2 dm$$, with radius of gyration $$k = \sqrt{I/M}$$. Mass far from the axis dominates I.

nodes.label: Parallel Axis Theorem
nodes.note: Shifting from the centre of mass to a parallel axis adds $Md^2$: $$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$$. The CM axis always carries the smallest I.

nodes.label: Perpendicular Axis Theorem
nodes.note: For a planar lamina, the out-of-plane moment equals the sum of the two in-plane moments: $$I_z = I_x + I_y$$. This quickly yields, for a disc, $$I_z = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$$.

nodes.label: Standard Moments of Inertia
nodes.note: Memorise the hierarchy $$I_{ring} = MR^2,\quad I_{disc} = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2,\quad I_{solid\ sphere} = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2,\quad I_{rod} = \tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$$. Smaller $I/MR^2$ means the body rolls faster.

nodes.label: Cavity by Negative Mass
nodes.note: A body with a cavity is the superposition of the full body minus the removed part: $$I = I_{full} - I_{removed}$$. The cavity piece's own CM offset then uses the parallel-axis theorem.

nodes.label: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
nodes.note: Torque as the rotational force, the rotational second law, and rotational work-energy. Dynamics of a body when the line of action misses the centre.

nodes.label: Definition of Torque
nodes.note: Torque is the moment of force about a point: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F},\quad \tau = rF\sin\phi$$. Its lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of force.

nodes.label: Rotational Second Law
nodes.note: Net torque produces angular acceleration: $$\tau_{net} = I\alpha$$, with the constraint equations of the problem supplying $\alpha$. It is the direct analogue of $F = ma$.

nodes.label: Angular Impulse and Work
nodes.note: Impulse of torque changes angular momentum, and torque does work through angle: $$\int \tau\, dt = \Delta L,\quad W = \int \tau\, d\theta,\quad P = \tau\omega$$. These are the rotational analogues of impulse and work.

nodes.label: Rotational Kinetic Energy
nodes.note: A spinning body stores $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis this replaces $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$; compare energies of differently shaped wheels at equal $\omega$.

nodes.label: Couple
nodes.note: Two equal opposite parallel forces form a pure moment: $$\tau = F \times d$$, independent of the pivot chosen. A couple spins a body without translating its CM.

nodes.label: Unwinding Yo-Yo and Hanging Mass
nodes.note: For a hanging mass $m$ on a string wrapped around a disc, Newton plus $\tau = I\alpha$ give $$a = \frac{g}{1 + I/mR^2}$$. The disc's inertia slows the descent.

nodes.label: Angular Momentum
nodes.note: Definition, conservation, and classic applications like the cue-ball strike. Conserved whenever external torque vanishes, exactly like linear momentum.

nodes.label: Definition of L
nodes.note: Angular momentum about a point is $$\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times m\vec{v}$$, and for a rigid body $$L = I\omega$$. Its direction follows the right-hand rule about the pivot.

nodes.label: Conservation of L
nodes.note: With zero net external torque, angular momentum is conserved: $$\tau_{ext} = 0 \Rightarrow L = const,\quad I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$$. A skater pulling in her arms spins faster because $I$ drops.

nodes.label: Direction and Precession Idea
nodes.note: Torque changes L along its own direction: $$\vec{\tau} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$$. A spinning top precesses because gravity torques its angular momentum sideways, not downward.

nodes.label: Cue Ball Strike Height
nodes.note: A horizontal cue strike produces immediate pure rolling when $$h = \frac{R}{2}\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$$ above the centre, i.e. $7R/10$ for a solid sphere. Below this height the ball skids forward; above it, it back-spins.

nodes.label: Rolling Motion
nodes.note: Combined translation and rotation, the rolling constraint, instantaneous centre, incline dynamics, and energy partitioning. The richest rigid-body topic in JEE.

nodes.label: Konig's Theorem for KE
nodes.note: Total kinetic energy splits into CM translation and rotation about the CM: $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}I_{cm}\omega^2$$. Each part is computed independently, then added.

nodes.label: Pure Rolling Condition
nodes.note: Rolling without slipping locks translation to rotation: $$v_{cm} = \omega R,\quad a_{cm} = \alpha R$$. Static friction enforces it and does no net work on the contact point.

nodes.label: Instantaneous Centre of Rotation
nodes.note: The contact point is momentarily at rest and acts as the pivot: every point's speed is $v = \omega d$ where $d$ is its distance from the contact. The top of a rolling wheel moves at $2v_{cm}$.

nodes.label: Rolling Down an Incline
nodes.note: Combining $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$ with $fR = I\alpha$ gives $$a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/MR^2}$$. The race down the incline ranks ring last and solid sphere first.

nodes.label: Great Incline Race
nodes.note: Acceleration depends only on shape factor $\beta = I/MR^2$: smaller $\beta$ wins. Solid sphere ($2/5$) beats disc ($1/2$), which beats ring ($1$), independent of mass and radius.

nodes.label: Speed at the Base
nodes.note: Energy conservation gives $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + I/MR^2}}$$, and travel time follows from $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. No slipping means static friction, so mechanical energy is conserved.

nodes.label: Toppling versus Sliding
nodes.note: When a block tips over instead of sliding, set by geometry against friction. Decides the angle at which a block on an incline first gives way.

nodes.label: Normal Reaction Migration
nodes.note: As the incline steepens, the normal shifts toward the downhill edge: $$x = \frac{h}{2}\tan\theta$$-style balance of torques. Toppling begins when the normal reaches the lower corner.

nodes.label: Toppling vs Sliding Criterion
nodes.note: Sliding starts at $$\tan\theta = \mu_s$$ while toppling starts at $$\tan\theta = \frac{b}{h}$$ (base over height). The smaller of $\mu_s$ and $b/h$ decides the failure mode.

nodes.label: High-Yield Traps
nodes.note: Frequent exam pitfalls in rotational mechanics, gathered as quick diagnostics. Read after every problem for a one-line self-check.

nodes.label: Axis Choice Trap
nodes.note: Always write $\tau = I\alpha$ about an axis fixed in direction; for moving axes add the $M a_{cm} \times r$ correction. Mixing axes between L and alpha silently breaks conservation arguments.

nodes.label: Moment of Inertia Axis Trap
nodes.note: $I$ is always about a specified axis; quoting a single value without its axis is meaningless. Shift with $$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$$ only between parallel axes through the same orientation.

nodes.label: Rolling Energy Trap
nodes.note: In pure rolling on a fixed surface, static friction does no work, yet friction is essential to enforce $v = \omega R$. Do not add a $f \cdot s$ dissipation term.
